facts.raw_span: A 31-year-old male nursing student
history of axillary hyperhidrosis
excessive sweating of the buttocks, most severe at the intergluteal cleft and sacrum
previously treated his axillary condition successfully with 20% aluminum chloride
treatment of the intergluteal cleft and sacrum with aluminum chloride was unsuccessful
used absorbent pads yet continued to soak through his pants
consequently unable to attend work
Minor starch-iodine test was performed
Areas of significant sweating were identified in the sacral region (10 × 3-cm area) and intergluteal cleft (6 × 8-cm area)
a 10 × 3-cm grid was drawn on the sacrum and a 6 × 8-cm grid was drawn on the intergluteal cleft
with the outermost dots omitted

concepts.why: The patient has a history of axillary hyperhidrosis and is now experiencing excessive sweating of the buttocks.
The patient's excessive sweating is not caused by an underlying medical condition, suggesting primary hyperhidrosis.
The patient's excessive sweating is limited to specific areas, such as the intergluteal cleft and sacrum.
The patient has a history of axillary hyperhidrosis, which was successfully treated with aluminum chloride.
The patient is experiencing excessive sweating in the gluteal region, specifically the intergluteal cleft and sacrum.
The patient's excessive sweating is a symptom of an underlying sweating disorder.
The patient's excessive sweating and skin irritation may be related to dyshidrotic eczema.
The patient's excessive sweating may be related to a nervous system disorder, such as neurogenic hyperhidrosis.
It explains the excessive sweating in the buttocks area, particularly the intergluteal cleft and sacrum, which may be a compensatory response to the treated axillary hyperhidrosis.

rationales.F05: Unsuccessful treatment of intergluteal cleft and sacrum with aluminum chloride may indicate a different condition.
rationales.F09: The Minor starch-iodine test results confirm excessive sweating in the sacral and intergluteal regions.
